content: Quinine, marketed under the brand name Qualaquin, is a medication approved by the FDA for the treatment of malaria, a disease caused by parasites typically transmitted through mosquito bites. As of December 2006, Qualaquin is the only FDA-approved brand of quinine available in the United States. The FDA has banned the sale of all non-approved brands of quinine due to the risk of severe side effects or death. Quinine is not approved for uses other than treating malaria, and it should not be used for conditions like leg cramps, as this is not an FDA-approved indication. Quinine can cause serious or life-threatening side effects. It is essential to use this medication only as prescribed by a doctor. Do not purchase quinine online or from vendors outside the United States, as improper use or unsupervised administration can result in severe consequences, including death. Individuals with a history of allergic reactions to quinine or similar medications, such as mefloquine or quinidine, should not use this drug. Additionally, quinine is contraindicated in patients with conditions like Long QT syndrome, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, myasthenia gravis, or optic neuritis (inflammation of the optic nerve). If you experience symptoms such as a weak pulse, fainting, fever, confusion, pale or yellowed skin, dark urine, hearing or vision loss, purple spots under the skin, blistering or peeling skin rash, or reduced urination, contact your doctor immediately. These may indicate serious side effects. While no medication is 100% effective in treating malaria, it is crucial to follow your doctor’s instructions and complete the full course of treatment. If symptoms persist or return after completing the medication, consult your doctor. Before taking quinine, inform your healthcare provider if you have allergies to any drugs or if you have a history of heart disease, heart rhythm disorders, low potassium levels (hypokalemia), or kidney or liver disease. Pregnant women should be aware that quinine is classified as FDA pregnancy category C, meaning it may harm an unborn baby. Pregnant women taking quinine are at a higher risk of hypoglycemia (low blood sugar), which can present as hunger, headache, confusion, irritability, drowsiness, weakness, dizziness, tremors, sweating, or a rapid heartbeat. Discuss your specific risks with your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Quinine may also pass into breast milk and could harm a nursing baby, so inform your doctor if you are breastfeeding. This medication is not recommended for children under 16 years of age. Take quinine exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Do not take larger doses or use it for longer than recommended. To reduce stomach upset, take the medication with food. If your malaria symptoms do not improve after two days of treatment or if they return after completing the medication, contact your doctor. Do not stop taking the medication early without consulting your doctor, as this may require alternative malaria prevention measures. If you are scheduled for surgery, inform your surgeon that you are taking quinine, as you may need to temporarily stop the medication. Quinine can interfere with certain medical tests, so ensure all healthcare providers are aware of your use of this drug. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is more than four hours past the scheduled time, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular dosing schedule. Do not take extra medication to make up for a missed dose. In the event of an overdose, seek emergency medical attention immediately. Symptoms of overdose may include headache, confusion, dizziness, ringing in the ears, vision or hearing loss, severe nausea or vomiting, sweating, uneven heart rate, light-headedness, fainting, or collapse. Avoid using quinine for any condition not prescribed by your doctor. Do not purchase it from unverified sources, as improper use can lead to severe side effects or death. Quinine may impair your thinking or reactions, so exercise caution when driving or performing tasks that require alertness. Avoid using antacids without your doctor’s advice, as some antacids can interfere with the absorption of quinine. Serious side effects of quinine include uneven heart rhythm, weak pulse, fainting, fever, confusion, pale or yellowed skin, dark urine, unusual muscle weakness, purple spots under the skin, reduced urination, severe blistering or peeling skin rash, severe nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, diarrhea, or problems with hearing or vision. If you experience any of these, stop using the medication and contact your doctor immediately. Less serious side effects may include hunger, headache, confusion, irritability, sweating, drowsiness, weakness, dizziness, tremors, or a warm, red, or tingling sensation under the skin. Report any unusual or bothersome side effects to your doctor. Quinine may interact with other medications, including antibiotics, heart rhythm medications, psychiatric drugs, narcotics, seizure medications, and other anti-malarial drugs. Inform your doctor about all prescription and over-the-counter medications, vitamins, minerals, herbal products, and other drugs you are taking. Do not start a new medication without consulting your doctor. For more information about quinine, consult your pharmacist or healthcare provider. Quinine is available by prescription under the brand name Qualaquin, and other generic forms may also be available. Always keep this and all other medications out of the reach of children, never share your medications with others, and use this medication only for the condition prescribed. If you have any questions about this medication, consult your doctor, nurse, or pharmacist.
